units.title: Present simple and present continuous
notes: Present simple for habits, routines and facts: My aunt works in a bank. With he, she and it add -s or -es: she watches.
Negatives and questions use do or does: He doesn't eat meat. Does she live here?
Present continuous (am, is, are + -ing) for things happening now or around now: Look, it is snowing.
Verbs like know, like, want and understand are not normally used in the continuous: I know him.

items.q: My elderly neighbour ___ his dog in the park every morning.
items.why: every morning is a routine, and he takes -s

items.q: Be careful! That careless driver ___ at the road.
items.why: it is happening now, so is + not + -ing

items.q: ___ your teenage brother usually tidy his room?
items.why: your brother is he, so Does

items.q: Why ___ you laughing? It isn't funny.
items.why: present continuous question with you needs are

items.q: Our new teacher is friendly, but she ___ rude students.
items.why: like is not used in the continuous, and she takes doesn't

items.q: Shy people often ___ speaking in front of the class.
items.why: people is plural, and hate is not used in the continuous

items.q: I ___ what you mean. Can you explain it again?
items.why: understand is not used in the continuous

items.q: Marta's hair is usually curly, but this week she ___ it straight.
items.why: this week is a temporary situation

items.q: How often ___ your grandparents visit you?
items.why: your grandparents is they, so do

items.q: Look at Dan! He ___ (wear) a really funny hat today.
items.why: Look! and today show it is happening now

items.q: My sister is very polite. She always ___ (say) thank you.
items.why: always shows a habit, and she takes -s

items.q: We ___ (not have) lessons on Sundays, so I sleep late.
items.why: a routine in the negative uses don't

items.q: Please turn the music down. I ___ (try) to study for an exam.
items.why: it is happening at the moment of speaking

items.q: My cheerful uncle ___ (watch) comedy films every Friday night.
My cousins ___ (not listen) to the teacher right now. They are chatting.
items.why: right now needs the present continuous

items.q: My dad have dark curly hair.
a: My dad has dark curly hair.

items.q: I am not knowing that good-looking actor.
a: I don't know that good-looking actor.
I do not know that good-looking actor.
items.why: know is not used in the continuous

items.q: Does she plays tennis on Saturdays?
a: Does she play tennis on Saturdays?
items.why: after does use the infinitive without -s

items.q: is / why / so miserable / looking / today / your friend
a: Why is your friend looking so miserable today?

items.q: at the weekend / early / never / my brother / gets up
a: My brother never gets up early at the weekend.
At the weekend my brother never gets up early.
items.why: never goes before the main verb

units.title: Past simple
notes: Regular verbs add -ed: walked, danced, carried, stopped. The form is the same for every person.
Many common verbs are irregular: go and went, buy and bought, take and took, wear and wore.
Negatives and questions use didn't or did + infinitive: I didn't go. Did you go?
The verb be has was and were and does not use did: Were you at home?

items.q: Yesterday I ___ a second-hand jacket at the market.
___ you wear your brand new trainers to the party last night?
items.why: past simple questions use Did + infinitive

items.q: Last Saturday she ___ like any of the jeans in the shop.
items.why: past simple negative uses didn't + infinitive

items.q: Where ___ you last weekend? I phoned you twice.
items.why: the verb be with you in the past is were

items.q: He ran so fast that he ___ the race easily.
We ___ at a café because it was raining heavily.
items.why: short vowel + consonant: double the p

items.q: My grandmother ___ very well-dressed when she was young.
What time ___ the fashion show start last night?
The shop assistant spoke politely and ___ me a bigger size.
Two years ago my cousin ___ (go) to London and bought some trendy clothes.
I ___ (not see) you at the party last night. Were you there?
Luckily, I ___ (study) hard last week, so the test was easy.
We ___ (be) very uncomfortable on the bus yesterday because it was so hot.
Mum ___ (take) the loose-fitting dress back to the shop last Monday.
They ___ (not be) at school yesterday because they were ill.
items.why: be does not use did: they weren't

items.q: Did you bought that casual shirt online?
a: Did you buy that casual shirt online?

items.q: I didn't went shopping last weekend.
a: I didn't go shopping last weekend.
I did not go shopping last weekend.

items.q: She weared a smart dress to the wedding.
a: She wore a smart dress to the wedding.

items.q: did / those / where / trendy / you / find / boots
a: Where did you find those trendy boots?

items.q: to school / yesterday / walked / quickly / we / very
a: We walked to school very quickly yesterday.
Yesterday we walked to school very quickly.
We walked very quickly to school yesterday.
Yesterday we walked very quickly to school.

units.title: Comparatives and superlatives
notes: Short adjectives: add -er and the -est: cheap, cheaper, the cheapest. Watch the spelling: big, bigger; easy, easier.
Long adjectives use more and the most: more difficult than, the most exciting.
Irregular: good, better, the best; bad, worse, the worst; far, further, the furthest.
Use than after a comparative, in after a superlative (the best in the class) and as ... as to say two things are equal.

items.q: My sister is ___ than me, so she left school first.
Getting a driving licence is ___ than I thought.
The day I got my degree was the ___ day of my life.
This exam was ___ than the last one. I failed it!
My grandad is the ___ person in our family. He is ninety.
Is going to university ___ expensive than getting a job?
Moving home is not as stressful ___ starting a new school.
She is the best student ___ the class.
items.why: after a superlative use in with places and groups

items.q: Today is ___ than yesterday, so take off your coat.
items.why: one vowel + one consonant: double the t

items.q: My new job is ___ (good) than my old one. I love it.
My brother got a job in the ___ (big) company in Spain.
items.why: the + superlative, and double the g

items.q: Maths is ___ (easy) than physics for me, so I get higher marks.
That was the ___ (boring) lesson of the whole year.
My cousin lives ___ (far) from school than I do, so she takes the bus.
People today retire ___ (late) than they did fifty years ago.
My dad is more tall than my uncle.
a: My dad is taller than my uncle.

items.q: She is the most young teacher in the school.
a: She is the youngest teacher in the school.

items.q: My brother is older that me.
a: My brother is older than me.

items.q: in / is / my family / the youngest / person / my cousin
a: My cousin is the youngest person in my family.
The youngest person in my family is my cousin.

items.q: more / than / is / getting a degree / getting a job / important
a: Getting a degree is more important than getting a job.
Getting a job is more important than getting a degree.

units.title: Past continuous
notes: Form: was or were + verb-ing. I was reading. They were laughing.
Negative: wasn't or weren't + -ing. Questions: Was she sleeping? Short answers: Yes, she was. No, she wasn't.
Use it for an action in progress at a moment in the past: At nine o'clock last night we were having dinner.
Spelling: run, running; swim, swimming; cycle, cycling.

items.q: At six o'clock yesterday we ___ volleyball on the beach.
items.why: an action in progress in the past: were + -ing

items.q: ___ your coach watching when you scored the point?
items.why: your coach is he or she, so Was

items.q: 'Were you jogging at seven this morning?' 'No, I ___.'
items.why: short answer with I uses wasn't

items.q: The players ___ listening to the trainer, so they made mistakes.
items.why: the players is they, so weren't

items.q: What ___ your sister doing at the gym at ten last night?
items.why: your sister is she, so was

items.q: This time last week I ___ in the sea near Tarifa.
'Was it raining during the rugby match?' 'Yes, it ___.'
My friends ___ in the gym at eight yesterday evening.
All yesterday afternoon Tom ___ table tennis with his cousin.
At 9 pm last night Dad ___ (watch) the ice hockey final on TV.
items.why: an action in progress at 9 pm

items.q: At ten o'clock last night I ___ (not sleep). I was still doing exercise.
The sun ___ (shine) when we arrived at the tennis club.
This time yesterday my cousins ___ (climb) a mountain in the Pyrenees.
Why ___ (you run) so fast at seven this morning? Were you late?
items.why: question: were + subject + -ing, double the n

items.q: At midday the gymnasts ___ (not practise). They were having lunch.
The children was swimming in the lake at noon.
a: The children were swimming in the lake at noon.

items.q: She was runing in the park at eight o'clock.
a: She was running in the park at eight o'clock.

items.q: We were play squash at six yesterday.
a: We were playing squash at six yesterday.

items.q: at / were / what / doing / you / midnight / last night
a: What were you doing at midnight last night?
What were you doing last night at midnight?

items.q: wasn't / in the race / my brother / this time yesterday / cycling
a: My brother wasn't cycling in the race this time yesterday.
This time yesterday my brother wasn't cycling in the race.

units.title: Past simple and past continuous
notes: Past continuous is the longer action in progress. Past simple is the short action that interrupts it: I was having a shower when the phone rang.
when usually goes before the past simple action: We were sleeping when the burglar came in.
while usually goes before the past continuous action: While we were walking home, it started to rain.
Use the past simple for actions that happen one after another: He took the bag and ran away.

items.q: I was waiting for the bus when a pickpocket ___ my phone.
items.why: the short action that interrupts is past simple

items.q: While we ___ on the beach, a thief took our bags.
items.why: the longer action after while is past continuous

items.q: The burglar broke the window ___ the family were sleeping.
items.why: while + subject + verb; during goes before a noun

items.q: We were watching a film ___ we heard a strange noise downstairs.
items.why: when introduces the short past simple action

items.q: What ___ you doing when the police arrived?
When the alarm rang, the shoplifter dropped the bag and ___ out of the shop.
items.why: one action after another uses the past simple

items.q: She cut herself while she ___ vegetables.
items.why: she + was + -ing for the longer action

items.q: The vandals ___ graffiti on the wall when a police officer saw them.
items.why: the action in progress is past continuous, and vandals is plural

items.q: I ___ the thief's face because he was wearing a mask.
items.why: see is not used in the continuous here; didn't + infinitive

items.q: A hacker ___ (steal) my password while I was using the café's wifi.
items.why: the short finished action is past simple

items.q: My sister was walking home when she ___ (see) two men robbing a shop.
items.why: after when, the short action is past simple

items.q: While the guard ___ (sleep), the thieves took three paintings.
items.why: the longer action after while is past continuous

items.q: It ___ (rain) when we left the police station, so we took a taxi.
items.why: the rain was in progress when we left

items.q: Somebody stole our bikes yesterday. We ___ (not look) at that moment.
items.why: in progress at that moment: weren't + -ing

items.q: Dad was talking to himself when I ___ (come) into the kitchen.
items.why: the short action that interrupts is past simple

items.q: I was having a shower when the phone was ringing.
a: I was having a shower when the phone rang.
items.why: the short action after when is past simple

items.q: He was breaking his leg while he was skating.
a: He broke his leg while he was skating.
items.why: breaking a leg is a short finished action

items.q: During I was shopping, someone stole my purse.
a: While I was shopping, someone stole my purse.
When I was shopping, someone stole my purse.
items.why: use while before subject + verb, not during

items.q: the burglar / were / when / we / came in / sleeping
a: We were sleeping when the burglar came in.
When the burglar came in, we were sleeping.
items.why: continuous for the long action, simple after when

items.q: while / her bag / someone / she / took / was dancing
a: Someone took her bag while she was dancing.
While she was dancing, someone took her bag.

units.title: some, any, much, many, a lot of, a few, a little
notes: some in positive sentences and requests: some shops, some rice. any in negatives and most questions: There isn't any milk. Are there any buses?
much with uncountable nouns and many with plural nouns, mostly in negatives and questions: How much traffic? How many cars?
a lot of works with countable and uncountable nouns: a lot of people, a lot of rubbish.
a few + plural nouns (a few buses); a little + uncountable nouns (a little time).

items.q: There isn't ___ public transport in my village.
How ___ recycling bins are there in your street?
items.why: bins is a plural countable noun

items.q: There was ___ rubbish on the beach after the festival.
items.why: rubbish is uncountable, so not many or a few

items.q: We've only got ___ time before rush hour, so let's go now.
How ___ pollution is there in your city?
There are ___ green spaces near my flat, so I often go for a walk.
Only ___ people were waiting at the taxi rank.
items.why: people is a plural countable noun

items.q: Are there ___ bus stops near your apartment building?
There aren't ___ road signs on this street, so drivers get lost.
We don't have ___ (much / many) time. The bus leaves in two minutes.
There were ___ (a few / a little) traffic jams this morning, so I was late.
items.why: traffic jams is plural and countable

items.q: Can I have ___ (some / any) information about the speed limit here, please?
There weren't ___ (some / any) crowds in the city centre on Monday.
___ (How much / How many) post boxes are there in your town?
items.why: post boxes is plural and countable

items.q: I put ___ (a few / a little) milk in my coffee, but no sugar.
How many traffic is there in the morning?
a: How much traffic is there in the morning?

items.q: We haven't got some pedestrian crossings near the school.
a: We haven't got any pedestrian crossings near the school.

items.q: There are much cars in the city centre.
a: There are a lot of cars in the city centre.
There are many cars in the city centre.
There are lots of cars in the city centre.
items.why: cars is countable, so not much

items.q: aren't / in / green spaces / there / my city / many
a: There aren't many green spaces in my city.
In my city there aren't many green spaces.
items.why: many + plural noun in a negative

items.q: is / in / how much / the streets / there / graffiti
a: How much graffiti is there in the streets?
items.why: How much + uncountable noun + is there

units.title: have to, must and should
notes: have to + infinitive means it is necessary, often a rule. It changes: has to, had to, Do you have to?
must + infinitive without to also means it is necessary. It has no -s and no past form (use had to): I must phone Gran.
mustn't means it is not allowed. don't have to means it is not necessary: You mustn't shout. You don't have to pay.
should and shouldn't + infinitive give advice: You should say sorry.

items.q: You ___ tell anyone my secret. Promise me!
It's Saturday tomorrow, so I ___ get up early.
My brother ___ look after our little sister every Friday.
You had an argument with Ana. I think you ___ say sorry.
Last night we ___ stay at home because Dad was annoyed with us.
items.why: the past of must and have to is had to

items.q: ___ your sister have to do a lot of homework?
items.why: question with she: Does ... have to

items.q: You ___ be so rude to your sister. It makes her sad.
Students ___ use their phones in class. It's against the rules.
items.why: against the rules means not allowed

items.q: He ___ come round tonight if he is tired. We can get together tomorrow.
items.why: not necessary, and he takes doesn't

items.q: My best friend ___ (have to) wear a uniform at her new school.
Yesterday I ___ (have to) do my dad a favour and wash the car.
items.why: yesterday needs the past: had to

items.q: We ___ (not have to) pay. Entry to the youth club is free.
___ (you have to) help at home every day?
items.why: questions with have to use do

items.q: Tom ___ (not have to) cook tonight because his parents are getting a pizza.
You look tired. You ___ (should / shouldn't) go to bed so late.
You must to be polite to your classmates.
a: You must be polite to your classmates.

items.q: She should makes up with her friend.
a: She should make up with her friend.
items.why: after should the verb has no -s

items.q: Does he has to hang out with them?
a: Does he have to hang out with them?
items.why: after does use have, not has

items.q: to / with / don't / you / agree / have / me
a: You don't have to agree with me.

items.q: each other / friends / after / should / an argument / talk to
a: Friends should talk to each other after an argument.
After an argument, friends should talk to each other.

units.title: Future: be going to and present continuous
notes: Present continuous for fixed arrangements, usually with a time or place: We're meeting Carla at six.
be going to + infinitive for plans and intentions: I'm going to learn the guitar this year.
be going to also for predictions when you can see the evidence now: Watch out! That glass is going to fall.
Do not forget am, is or are: She is going to travel. Are you going to come?

items.q: We ___ off at six tomorrow morning. The taxi is booked.
Look at that long queue! We ___ miss our flight.
items.why: a prediction from what we can see now

items.q: ___ your dad going to pick us up from the airport?
items.why: your dad is he, so Is

items.q: I'm going to ___ around the shops before I go to the departure gate.
What time ___ you checking in tomorrow?
They ___ going to take much baggage. It's only a weekend trip.
'Are you going to go away this summer?' 'Yes, we ___.'
items.why: short answers repeat the verb be

items.q: My cousin ___ back from Dublin on Friday. I've seen her ticket.
Be careful! Your passport ___ out of your pocket.
The sky is completely black. There ___ (be) a storm.
items.why: a prediction from evidence uses going to

items.q: I've decided. I ___ (learn) some Italian before our trip to Rome.
We ___ (meet) Grandma in the baggage hall at ten. She knows the plan.
items.why: an arrangement with a time and place

items.q: He ___ (not come) with us on Saturday. He has decided to stay at home.
Slow down! You ___ (drop) all those bags!
items.why: you can see it is about to happen

items.q: ___ (she fly) to Paris tomorrow? I saw her boarding pass on the table.
I going to show my passport at passport control.
a: I am going to show my passport at passport control.
I'm going to show my passport at passport control.

items.q: She is going to buys a magazine for the flight.
a: She is going to buy a magazine for the flight.

items.q: We meeting our friends at the check-in desk at nine.
a: We are meeting our friends at the check-in desk at nine.
We're meeting our friends at the check-in desk at nine.

items.q: to / are / what / you / in London / going / do
a: What are you going to do in London?
items.why: question word + are + subject + going to

items.q: at / is / tomorrow / taking off / seven o'clock / our plane
a: Our plane is taking off at seven o'clock tomorrow.
Our plane is taking off tomorrow at seven o'clock.
Tomorrow our plane is taking off at seven o'clock.
At seven o'clock tomorrow our plane is taking off.

units.title: Present perfect
notes: Form: have or has + past participle. I've finished. She hasn't arrived. Have they eaten?
Regular participles end in -ed. Irregular ones must be learned: see, saw, seen; give, gave, given; spend, spent, spent.
Use it for past actions connected to now, when the exact time is not said: I've lost my receipt (I can't find it now).
been means went and came back. gone means went and is still there: She has gone to the bank.

items.q: I ___ my receipt, so I can't take the shoes back.
My sister ___ up enough money for a new phone.
___ you ever opened a bank account?
items.why: present perfect question with you uses Have

items.q: We ___ paid for the tickets. We'll do it tomorrow.
'Has the price gone up?' 'Yes, it ___.'
Dad isn't here. He has ___ to the bank.
items.why: gone means he is still there

items.q: I have never ___ so much money in one day!
items.why: the participle of spend is spent

items.q: I've ___ to that shopping centre three times. It's great.
items.why: been means I went and came back

items.q: She has ___ all her old toys away to a charity shop.
items.why: the participle of give is given

items.q: Look! Somebody ___ (leave) their change at the checkout.
items.why: a past action with a result now

items.q: My parents ___ (never buy) anything online. They prefer real shops.
items.why: never goes between have and the participle

items.q: I can't buy the game because I ___ (not save) enough money.
___ (you ever pay) for something with your phone?
items.why: ever + present perfect for life experience

items.q: I ___ (already pay) for the pizzas, so put your money away.
items.why: already goes between have and the participle

items.q: Prices ___ (go) up a lot this year.
items.why: this year is not finished, so present perfect

items.q: He have spent all his pocket money.
a: He has spent all his pocket money.

items.q: I have never saw such a big special offer.
a: I have never seen such a big special offer.
items.why: the participle of see is seen

items.q: Has she took the jeans back to the shop?
a: Has she taken the jeans back to the shop?
items.why: the participle of take is taken

items.q: ever / a wallet / have / found / you / in the street
a: Have you ever found a wallet in the street?

items.q: hasn't / the / my brother / opened / from the bank / letter
a: My brother hasn't opened the letter from the bank.

units.title: Present perfect and past simple; How long, for and since
notes: Present perfect for experiences up to now with no finished time: I've tried sushi.
Past simple with finished time words (yesterday, last year, in 2020, two days ago): I tried sushi last summer.
How long + present perfect for situations that started in the past and continue now: How long have you lived here?
for + a period of time (for two years); since + the starting point (since 2019, since Monday).

items.q: I ___ sushi for the first time last summer.
items.why: last summer is a finished time

items.q: We have lived in this flat ___ 2019.
How long ___ you known your best friend?
items.why: you still know your friend, so present perfect

items.q: My grandparents have been married ___ fifty years.
items.why: fifty years is a period of time

items.q: When ___ you cook that delicious soup?
items.why: When asks about a finished time, so past simple

items.q: She ___ raw fish. She doesn't want to try it.
He has worked in that restaurant ___ last March.
items.why: last March is the starting point

items.q: I ___ a really spicy curry two days ago.
'Have you ever tasted frozen yoghurt?' 'Yes, I ___ some last week.'
items.why: last week is a finished time

items.q: We ___ (eat) at that Italian restaurant last Friday. The pizza was tasty.
items.why: last Friday is a finished time

items.q: I ___ (have) this recipe book since my birthday.
items.why: since + a situation that continues now

items.q: My mum ___ (make) a delicious cake yesterday, but it has all gone now.
Carla ___ (be) a vegetarian for three years, and she still feels great.
items.why: it started in the past and continues now

items.q: How long ___ (you have) that fridge? It looks very old.
They ___ (open) the new café in 2022.
I have eaten a sour apple yesterday.
a: I ate a sour apple yesterday.

items.q: We are friends since primary school.
a: We have been friends since primary school.
We've been friends since primary school.

items.q: She has lived here since two years.
a: She has lived here for two years.
items.why: use for with a period of time

items.q: you / long / have / how / in Spain / lived
a: How long have you lived in Spain?

items.q: for / haven't / I / chocolate / eaten / a month
a: I haven't eaten chocolate for a month.

units.title: will and be going to
notes: will or won't + infinitive for predictions and opinions, often after I think, I'm sure, probably: I'm sure you'll feel better.
will also for decisions made at the moment of speaking, offers and promises: I'll get you some water.
be going to for plans you decided before speaking: I'm going to see the doctor on Monday.
be going to for predictions when you can see the evidence now: Look out! You're going to fall.

items.q: 'I've got a terrible headache.' 'Sit down. I ___ you some water.'
items.why: an offer decided at the moment of speaking

items.q: I've already phoned the doctor. I ___ her at five o'clock.
I'm sure you ___ better after a good sleep.
Be careful on that wall! You ___ your ankle.
items.why: a prediction from what you can see now

items.q: Don't worry. The injection ___ hurt.
items.why: a promise or prediction: won't + infinitive

items.q: ___ doctors find a cure for the flu one day?
items.why: a question about a future prediction

items.q: She will probably ___ a cold if she goes out with wet hair.
I promise I ___ you in hospital every day.
He has bought new running shoes because he ___ get fit this year.
Perhaps my knee ___ (be) better next week. I hope so.
items.why: a prediction with perhaps uses will

items.q: I think I ___ (not go) to school tomorrow. I still have a fever.
items.why: an opinion about the future uses won't

items.q: Look at him on that skateboard! He ___ (fall)!
items.why: you can see the evidence now

items.q: Mum made the appointment last week. She ___ (take) me to the dentist on Monday because of my toothache.
'I can't open this bottle of cough medicine.' 'Give it to me. I ___ (open) it for you.'
items.why: an offer at the moment of speaking

items.q: In the future, I'm sure people ___ (not get) ill so often.
I think she wills get better soon.
a: I think she will get better soon.
I think she'll get better soon.

items.q: Don't worry, I will to look after you.
a: Don't worry, I will look after you.
Don't worry, I'll look after you.

items.q: He is going break his arm if he is not careful.
a: He is going to break his arm if he is not careful.
He's going to break his arm if he is not careful.

items.q: will / you / soon / feel / I'm sure / better
a: I'm sure you will feel better soon.
I'm sure you will soon feel better.

items.q: going / see / I'm / a doctor / to / about my back
a: I'm going to see a doctor about my back.

units.title: Modals of probability: must, might, could, can't
notes: must + infinitive means I'm almost sure it is true: You've run ten kilometres. You must be thirsty.
might or could + infinitive means it is possible: Take an umbrella. It might rain.
can't + infinitive means I'm almost sure it is not true: That can't be a shark. (Do not use mustn't here.)
These modals never change form and have no to after them: She might be at home.

items.q: That animal has big ears and flies at night. It ___ be a bat.
items.why: the evidence makes you almost sure

items.q: It ___ be a shark. Sharks don't live in rivers!
items.why: you are sure it is impossible

items.q: I'm not sure what made that noise. It ___ be a fox.
items.why: not sure means it is only possible

items.q: She might ___ afraid of bees. I don't really know.
Take some cream with you. There ___ be mosquitoes near the lake.
The eagle has been flying all day. It ___ be tired.
items.why: you are almost sure it is true

items.q: He ___ be at the zoo. I saw him at home two minutes ago.
items.why: you are sure it is not true

items.q: Perhaps the deer are hiding. They ___ come out later.
This insect has colourful wings, so it ___ a butterfly.
items.why: must has no -s and no to

items.q: I'm sure that isn't a worm. It's much too big. It ___ (must / might / can't) be a worm.
Perhaps there are frogs in this pond. There ___ (must / might / can't) be frogs in this pond.
I'm certain the donkey is hungry. It ___ (must / could / can't) be hungry.
It's possible that the fox lives under our shed. It ___ (must / could / can't) live there.
It is possible that the ants won't come back. They ___ (might not / can't / must) come back.
You saw a wolf in the city centre? You ___ (must / might / can't) be serious!
That must to be an eagle.
It mights be a fly or a bee.
a: It might be a fly or a bee.

items.q: That mustn't be a shark. We are in a swimming pool!
a: That can't be a shark. We are in a swimming pool!
items.why: use can't when you are sure it is not true

items.q: be / a wolf / outside / there / might / the tent
a: There might be a wolf outside the tent.

items.q: must / very tired / flying / after / be / the birds / all day
a: The birds must be very tired after flying all day.
After flying all day, the birds must be very tired.

units.title: Present perfect with just, already and yet
notes: just means a very short time ago. It goes between have or has and the participle: The bus has just left.
already means before now or sooner than expected. It goes between have or has and the participle: I've already seen it.
yet goes at the end of negatives and questions: I haven't finished yet. Have you finished yet?

items.q: I haven't told my parents about my exam result ___.
items.why: yet goes at the end of a negative

items.q: She's exhausted because she has ___ run ten kilometres.
items.why: just means a very short time ago

items.q: 'Shall I explain it again?' 'No, thanks. You've ___ explained it twice.'
Have you finished that boring book ___?
items.why: yet goes at the end of a question

items.q: We ___ heard the news. We are amazed!
He hasn't said sorry ___, so I'm still annoyed.
It's only nine o'clock and I've ___ done all my homework. I'm so proud!
My sister has just ___ her driving test, so she's very relaxed now.
'Is Dad still here?' 'No, he ___. You missed him by a minute.'
items.why: just goes between has and the participle

items.q: The match ___ (just finish). The players are still on the pitch.
I ___ (not see) my exam results yet, so I feel stressed.
items.why: yet needs the present perfect negative

items.q: We ___ (already buy) the tickets, so you don't need to queue.
___ (you tidy) your room yet? Grandma arrives in an hour.
items.why: question with yet uses the present perfect

items.q: Don't be scared. The spider ___ (just go) out of the window.
Lucy ___ (not reply) to my message yet. I feel a bit disappointed.
She has just arrive at the station.
a: She has just arrived at the station.

items.q: We already have seen this embarrassing video.
a: We have already seen this embarrassing video.
We've already seen this embarrassing video.
We have seen this embarrassing video already.

items.q: I didn't finish my homework yet.
a: I haven't finished my homework yet.
I have not finished my homework yet.
items.why: yet is used with the present perfect

items.q: haven't / the / yet / results / they / announced
a: They haven't announced the results yet.

items.q: has / a / my brother / won / just / prize
a: My brother has just won a prize.
items.why: just goes between has and the participle

units.title: Relative clauses: who, which, that, where
notes: A relative clause tells us which person, thing or place we mean: The girl who sits next to me is from Peru.
who or that for people: an actor who plays a detective. which or that for things: a film which makes me laugh.
where for places: This is the cinema where we saw the film.
Do not repeat the subject or object: the film that I watched (not the film that I watched it).

items.q: A director is a person ___ makes films.
This is the soap opera ___ my grandma watches every day.
That's the cinema ___ we saw the horror film.
I love documentaries ___ teach me about animals.
The actor ___ plays the main character is from Seville.
Is this the studio ___ they film the chat show?
I didn't like the review ___ I read online.
The woman ___ reads the news is very serious.
items.why: that can be used for people

items.q: That is the series which ___ about a teenage detective.
items.why: which is already the subject, so no it

items.q: A comedian is someone ___ (who / which / where) tells jokes on TV.
Let's go to the café ___ (who / which / where) we met the actors.
The trailer ___ (who / which / where) I watched yesterday was really exciting.
She is the presenter ___ (who / which / where) won the prize last year.
The soundtrack ___ (who / that / where) you are listening to is from a science fiction film.
This is the town ___ (who / which / where) they made the period drama.
items.why: they made it there, so where

items.q: That's the animation that I watched it last night.
a: That's the animation that I watched last night.
That's the animation which I watched last night.
That's the animation I watched last night.
items.why: that replaces it, so do not repeat it

items.q: He is the actor which won the prize.
a: He is the actor who won the prize.
He is the actor that won the prize.
items.why: who or that for people, not which

items.q: She's the girl who she plays the detective.
a: She's the girl who plays the detective.
items.why: who is the subject, so no second she

items.q: the man / my uncle / is / who / the crime drama / wrote
a: The man who wrote the crime drama is my uncle.
My uncle is the man who wrote the crime drama.

items.q: the clip / was / you / very funny / that / sent me
a: The clip that you sent me was very funny.

units.title: Present simple passive
notes: Form: am, is or are + past participle. Rice is grown in Asia. These cars are made in Germany.
Negative: isn't or aren't + participle. Question: Is French spoken in Canada?
Use the passive when the action is more important than who does it, or when we don't know who does it.
Use by to say who does the action: This app is used by millions of people.

items.q: Millions of photos ___ every day.
This app ___ by teenagers all over the world.
items.why: the app does not use, it is used

items.q: ___ the computers switched off at night?
items.why: plural subject in a passive question

items.q: The school website ___ updated at weekends.
These phones are ___ in South Korea.
Where ___ this podcast recorded?
A lot of videos are shared ___ young people.
items.why: by shows who does the action

items.q: Old files ___ automatically after thirty days.
items.why: files do not delete, they are deleted

items.q: 'Is the wifi turned off at night?' 'No, it ___.'
items.why: short answers repeat the verb be

items.q: The lights in our classroom ___ (turn off) at five o'clock every day.
Spanish ___ (speak) in more than twenty countries.
items.why: the participle of speak is spoken

items.q: Mobile phones ___ (not allow) in our exams.
This laptop ___ (sell) with a free bag in all the shops.
items.why: the participle of sell is sold

items.q: How many apps ___ (install) on a new phone in the factory?
The projector ___ (not use) very often because it is old.
The links is shared with all the students.
a: The links are shared with all the students.

items.q: This game is play by millions of people.
a: This game is played by millions of people.

items.q: Our computers are checked for viruses from an expert.
a: Our computers are checked for viruses by an expert.
items.why: use by for the person who does the action

items.q: in / made / are / these tablets / China
a: These tablets are made in China.

items.q: is / off / the computer / every night / switched / why
a: Why is the computer switched off every night?

units.title: Zero and first conditional
notes: Zero conditional: if + present simple, present simple. Use it for things that are always true: If you mix blue and yellow, you get green.
First conditional: if + present simple, will or won't + infinitive. Use it for a real possibility in the future: If it rains, we'll stay in.
Never use will in the if-clause: If it rains (not If it will rain).
unless means if not: We won't finish unless we hurry.

items.q: If you boil water, it ___ into steam.
items.why: always true: present simple, and it takes -s

items.q: Be careful! If you shake that bottle, the cola ___ out when you open it.
If it ___ tomorrow, we will do the experiment inside.
items.why: present simple after if, and it takes -s

items.q: We won't finish the experiment ___ we work faster.
If you don't stir the soup now, it ___ burn.
Ice ___ if you take it out of the freezer.
If you ___ the jar with a cloth, the insects won't escape.
Plants die if they ___ enough water.
items.why: zero conditional: present simple, and they takes don't

items.q: Unless you ___ the rope tightly, the box will open.
If you mix red and white, you always ___ (get) pink.
items.why: always true: present simple in both parts

items.q: If our teacher ___ (let) us, we will carry out the experiment tomorrow.
You ___ (not pass) the science test next week if you don't work out the answers yourself.
If you ___ (not wrap) the ice in paper, it will melt before lunchtime.
When you rub your hands together, they always ___ (become) warm.
If you drop that glass jar in class tomorrow, the teacher ___ (be) angry.
If it will be sunny tomorrow, we will do the experiment outside.
a: If it is sunny tomorrow, we will do the experiment outside.
If it's sunny tomorrow, we will do the experiment outside.

items.q: If you heat butter, it melt.
a: If you heat butter, it melts.

items.q: Unless you don't add up the numbers carefully, you will make a mistake.
a: Unless you add up the numbers carefully, you will make a mistake.
If you don't add up the numbers carefully, you will make a mistake.

items.q: it / you / if / falls / a ball / drop
a: If you drop a ball, it falls.
A ball falls if you drop it.
It falls if you drop a ball.
items.why: zero conditional: present simple in both parts

items.q: we / if / will / hurry / be late / don't / we
a: If we don't hurry, we will be late.
We will be late if we don't hurry.

units.title: Reported commands and requests
notes: Reporting verb + person + to + infinitive: 'Sit down!' becomes The teacher told us to sit down.
For negatives use not to + infinitive: 'Don't shout!' becomes She told them not to shout.
tell for orders, ask for polite requests, advise for advice. Also warn, remind, persuade, encourage.
tell and ask need a person with no to: He told me to wait (not He said me, not He told to me).

items.q: The guide told us ___ the paintings.
The director asked the actors ___ earlier the next day.
My art teacher ___ me to use more colourful paint.
'Please be quiet.' The poet asked the audience ___ quiet.
The writer advised ___ to read a lot of novels.
'Don't forget your tickets!' Mum reminded us ___ our tickets.
'Give me your pencil.' She told me to give her ___ pencil.
items.why: your changes to my in the report

items.q: The guard warned the children ___ near the sculpture.
Our teacher encouraged us ___ the gallery at the weekend.
'Open your books.' The teacher told us ___ (open) our books.
'Don't take photos.' The guard told the visitors ___ (not take) photos.
I asked the novelist ___ (sign) my copy of her book, and she did.
'You should visit the studio.' My friend advised me ___ (visit) the studio.
The museum guide warned the tourists ___ (not sit) on the historical chairs.
My parents persuaded me ___ (study) art at university. Now I'm a successful painter.
The teacher said us to write a poem.
a: The teacher told us to write a poem.

items.q: She told me to not be late for the concert.
a: She told me not to be late for the concert.

items.q: He asked to me to close the studio door.
a: He asked me to close the studio door.

items.q: to / the director / quiet / told / be / everyone
a: The director told everyone to be quiet.

items.q: asked / not / her / to / me / my sister / use / paints
a: My sister asked me not to use her paints.

units.title: Second conditional
notes: Form: if + past simple, would or wouldn't + infinitive. If I had a boat, I would sail around the world.
Use it for imaginary or unlikely situations in the present or future. It does not talk about the past.
Never use would in the if-clause: If I knew (not If I would know).
If I were you, I'd ... is used to give advice. The short form of would is 'd.

items.q: If he ___ taller, he would be a great goalkeeper.
If she had more free time, she ___ as a babysitter.
What ___ you do if you were a politician?
I wouldn't take that job if I ___ you.
items.why: If I were you is used for advice

items.q: If my brother ___ harder, he could be a lawyer.
I ___ be a vet if I were afraid of animals.
If we ___ in a bigger city, there would be more jobs.
Would you be a firefighter if the job ___ so dangerous?
If journalists didn't ask questions, we ___ the truth.
If I ___ (have) a lot of money, I would open my own hairdresser's.
If she were a film director, she ___ (make) comedies.
He ___ (not be) so tired if he didn't work as a cleaner at night.
If you ___ (can) have any job in the world, what would you choose?
items.why: the past of can is could

items.q: Where ___ (you work) if you were an architect?
If my dad ___ (not be) a pharmacist, he would be a scientist.
items.why: past simple of be after if

items.q: If I would have more time, I would write a novel.
a: If I had more time, I would write a novel.
If I had more time, I'd write a novel.

items.q: If he was a presenter, he will be on TV every day.
a: If he was a presenter, he would be on TV every day.
If he were a presenter, he would be on TV every day.

items.q: I would to be an artist if I could paint well.
a: I would be an artist if I could paint well.
I'd be an artist if I could paint well.

items.q: would / if / a scientist / I / I / be / were good at maths
a: If I were good at maths, I would be a scientist.
I would be a scientist if I were good at maths.

items.q: you / a blogger / what / write about / would / if / you were
a: What would you write about if you were a blogger?
If you were a blogger, what would you write about?
items.why: would + subject + infinitive in the question

units.title: Reported speech
notes: The verb moves one step back: present simple to past simple, present continuous to past continuous, will to would, can to could.
'I like jazz,' said Ben. Ben said (that) he liked jazz. The word that is optional.
Pronouns and possessives change: 'I'll call my mum,' said Eva. Eva said she would call her mum.
say something, but tell somebody something: He said he was tired. He told me he was tired.

items.q: 'I like graphic novels,' said Leo. Leo said he ___ graphic novels.
items.why: present simple moves back to past simple

items.q: She ___ me that the article was interesting.
He ___ that he couldn't find the brochure.
items.why: say has no person after it

items.q: 'We are making a poster,' they said. They said they ___ a poster.
items.why: present continuous moves back to past continuous

items.q: 'I will write you a note,' said Mum. Mum said she ___ write me a note.
'I can speak three languages,' said Eva. Eva said she ___ speak three languages.
'I love my new e-book,' said Ana. Ana said she loved ___ new e-book.
'We don't read the paper,' they said. They said they ___ the paper.
My teacher told ___ that my article was very good.
'I work for a newspaper,' said Tom. Tom said he ___ (work) for a newspaper.
items.why: present simple moves back to past simple

items.q: 'I am reading a great e-book,' said Sara. Sara said she ___ (read) a great e-book.
items.why: am reading moves back to was reading

items.q: 'We will put up the posters,' they said. They said they ___ (put) up the posters.
'I can't see the notice,' said Dan. Dan said he ___ (not can) see the notice.
'I don't want any stickers,' said the boy. The boy said he ___ (not want) any stickers.
items.why: don't want moves back to didn't want

items.q: 'I won't tell anyone,' said Paul. Paul said he ___ (not tell) anyone.
She said me that the advert was funny.
a: She told me that the advert was funny.
She said that the advert was funny.
She said to me that the advert was funny.
items.why: tell + person, or say without a person

items.q: He said he will send me the article.
a: He said he would send me the article.
items.why: will changes to would after said

items.q: Marta told that she was writing a note.
a: Marta said that she was writing a note.
Marta told me that she was writing a note.
items.why: tell needs a person after it

items.q: she / said / the brochure / that / was / my aunt / reading
a: My aunt said that she was reading the brochure.

items.q: told / would / us / help / he / the teacher / us
a: The teacher told us he would help us.
He told us the teacher would help us.

units.title: Past simple passive
notes: Form: was or were + past participle. The bridge was built in 1900. The windows were broken.
Negative: wasn't or weren't + participle. Question: Was the thief caught? When were they built?
Use it when the action is more important than who did it, or when we don't know who did it: My bike was stolen.
Use by to say who did the action: It was painted by Picasso.

items.q: The first photograph ___ in 1826.
These paintings ___ by a teenage artist.
___ the film watched by many people?
My phone ___ stolen. I found it under the sofa.
The Mona Lisa was painted ___ Leonardo da Vinci.
items.why: by shows who did the action

items.q: When ___ these houses built?
The thief ___ by a neighbour last night.
We ___ a hint by the teacher, so the puzzle was easier.
'Was the letter sent yesterday?' 'Yes, it ___.'
This bridge ___ (build) more than two hundred years ago.
The windows ___ (break) during the storm last night.
I ___ (not invite) to the party last Saturday, so I stayed at home.
The first Harry Potter book ___ (write) in the 1990s.
items.why: the participle of write is written

items.q: Where ___ (the keys find) yesterday? I looked everywhere!
The students ___ (not tell) about the test until Friday morning.
The song was sang by the whole class.
a: The song was sung by the whole class.
items.why: the participle of sing is sung

items.q: Three people was hurt in the accident.
a: Three people were hurt in the accident.

items.q: My bike stolen last week.
a: My bike was stolen last week.

items.q: in / was / this school / 1985 / opened
were / who / by / taken / these photos
a: Who were these photos taken by?
